name: Nietzsche's contempt for women
plain_explanation: Nietzsche repeatedly and harshly disparages women, treating them as incapable of friendship, existing chiefly for men's 'recreation,' and dangerous once granted independence from male control; Russell treats this less as a serious argument than as a revealing symptom of Nietzsche's own psychology.
precise_definition: A recurring element of Nietzsche's ethics, expressed in passages from Thus Spake Zarathustra ('Man shall be trained for war and woman for the recreation of the warrior') and Beyond Good and Evil (recommending women be regarded 'as property, as Orientals do'), offered by Nietzsche as self-evident rather than argued from evidence.
why_it_mattered: Russell uses it as a case study in how Nietzsche's stated doctrines can be read as 'objectification[s] of his own emotion,' arguing Nietzsche's fierce misogyny masks fear -- 'nine women out of ten would get the whip away from him, and he knew it.'
historical_origin: Thus Spake Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, The Will to Power.
examples: 'Thou goest to woman? Do not forget thy whip.'
Women described as 'not, as yet, capable of friendship; they are still cats, or birds, or at best cows.'
objections: Russell: 'it is not backed up by evidence from history or from his own experience, which, so far as women were concerned, was almost confined to his sister.'
